interactions.label: Three patients arrive simultaneously: a 2-year-old with stridor and cyanosis aft

params.question: Three patients arrive simultaneously: a 2-year-old with stridor and cyanosis after swallowing a coin, an adult with facial fractures and gurgling respirations, and a 55-year-old with bilateral epistaxis for 45 minutes. Using ABCDE triage, who is attended to first?

answers.text: The epistaxis patient — uncontrolled haemorrhage causes hypovolaemic shock fastest

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Epistaxis threatens circulation (C), not airway (A). In ABCDE, airway compromise with active hypoxia takes precedence over haemorrhage.

answers.text: The facial trauma patient — gurgling means the airway is already compromised

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gurgling indicates a compromised but partially patent airway. The child's cyanosis signals complete or near-complete obstruction with active oxygen desaturation, placing her higher in priority.

answers.text: The child with stridor and cyanosis — active hypoxia leads to cardiac arrest within minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Cyanosis indicates critical oxygen desaturation. In a child, cardiac arrest from hypoxia can occur within minutes. Begin back blows and chest thrusts immediately while preparing an emergency airway.

answers.text: All three simultaneously — divide the team equally among the patients

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dividing resources equally ignores the hierarchy of threats. The child's airway obstruction is the most time-critical; she must be attended first, with the facial trauma patient second and epistaxis third.

overallFeedback.feedback: In ABCDE triage, airway (A) takes priority over breathing (B) and circulation (C). The child's cyanosis with stridor indicates the most immediately life-threatening condition among the three.
Correct. Airway always comes first in ABCDE. Cyanosis with stridor signals imminent cardiac arrest — this patient cannot wait.

interactions.label: A 3-year-old has a foreign body in the right nostril. On anterior rhinoscopy you

params.question: A 3-year-old has a foreign body in the right nostril. On anterior rhinoscopy you can see the object but cannot safely pass a hook behind it. The correct action is to refer for removal under general anaesthesia. In which situation is this approach overridden?

answers.text: When the foreign body is a smooth plastic bead that has been present for less than one hour

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A plastic bead is inert. If you cannot safely hook it, referring for removal under GA is correct regardless of how recently it was inserted.

answers.text: When the child is calm and cooperative enough for a second attempt

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cooperation does not change the anatomy. If the hook cannot be safely passed behind the object, repeated blind attempts risk pushing it into the nasopharynx and potentially into the larynx.

answers.text: When the foreign body is a button battery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Button batteries cause electrical and chemical necrosis of mucosa within 1–2 hours. Immediate removal is mandatory regardless of conditions, because the tissue damage from waiting exceeds the procedural risk.

answers.text: When the foreign body has been present for more than 48 hours and secondary infection is developing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Infection around an inert foreign body can be managed with antibiotics while arranging safe removal under GA. The urgency of a button battery is not about infection but about ongoing chemical and electrical tissue destruction.

overallFeedback.feedback: The rule is: if you cannot see and safely hook the foreign body, stop and refer. The sole exception is a button battery — electrical and chemical necrosis begins within 1–2 hours, making immediate removal mandatory.
Correct. A button battery is the one foreign body that cannot wait — necrosis begins within 1–2 hours, so immediate removal is mandatory regardless of conditions.

interactions.label: A patient with chronic suppurative otitis media has a central perforation of the

params.question: A patient with chronic suppurative otitis media has a central perforation of the tympanic membrane. You need to prescribe topical ear drops. Which is the safest choice?

answers.text: Neomycin drops — broad-spectrum aminoglycoside effective against common pathogens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neomycin is an aminoglycoside. With a perforated TM, drops pass through the middle ear and contact the cochlea via the round window. Aminoglycosides are ototoxic and risk permanent sensorineural hearing loss.

answers.text: Ciprofloxacin drops — quinolones are not ototoxic at topical concentrations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Quinolone drops like ciprofloxacin are safe even with a perforated TM because they do not damage the cochlea at topical concentrations, unlike aminoglycosides.

answers.text: Gentamicin drops — first-line for Pseudomonas coverage in ear infections

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside. Although it is effective against Pseudomonas, it is ototoxic when it reaches the cochlea through a perforated tympanic membrane. Use a quinolone instead.

answers.text: Combined neomycin-polymyxin drops — dual coverage ensures faster resolution

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Any preparation containing neomycin is contraindicated with a perforated TM. The neomycin component passes through the perforation and damages the cochlea, regardless of what it is combined with.

overallFeedback.feedback: With a perforated TM, ear drops pass through the middle ear and reach the cochlea via the round window. Aminoglycosides (neomycin, gentamicin) are ototoxic at this site. Quinolones like ciprofloxacin are the safe choice.

Correct. When the tympanic membrane is perforated, drops reach the cochlea via the round window. Quinolones are safe; aminoglycosides (neomycin, gentamicin) are contraindicated because they are ototoxic.

interactions.label: When consenting a patient for mastoidectomy, stating that the risk of facial ner

params.question: When consenting a patient for mastoidectomy, stating that the risk of facial nerve injury is 'less than one percent' is sufficient, without describing that the consequence includes inability to close the eye and drooping of the mouth.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Stating frequency without consequence is specifically identified as the most dangerous consent error. A patient told 'less than one percent risk' without knowing it means possible permanent facial paralysis cannot make a truly informed decision. Always pair the number with what it means.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Frequency alone is never enough. The video identifies this as the most dangerous consent error. The patient must understand what the complication means for them — facial paralysis affecting eye closure and mouth movement — not just how rarely it occurs.

interactions.label: At a screening camp, a 35-year-old factory worker's audiogram shows a dip at 4 k

params.question: At a screening camp, a 35-year-old factory worker's audiogram shows a dip at 4 kHz with normal thresholds at adjacent frequencies. What is the correct interpretation and next step?

answers.text: Normal age-related presbycusis — reassure and retest in five years

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Presbycusis typically causes a gradual high-frequency slope, not an isolated notch at 4 kHz. A notch pattern in a noise-exposed worker points to noise-induced hearing loss, not ageing.

answers.text: Early noise-induced hearing loss — institute hearing protection and schedule follow-up audiometry

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The 4 kHz notch is the earliest audiometric sign of noise-induced hearing loss and is also the key marker for occupational compensation. The worker needs hearing protection immediately and periodic monitoring.

answers.text: Conductive hearing loss from chronic otitis media — refer for tympanometry

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Conductive hearing loss affects low to mid frequencies and shows an air-bone gap. An isolated 4 kHz notch with normal bone conduction is the hallmark of sensorineural damage from noise exposure.

answers.text: Equipment artefact — repeat the test before taking any action

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A 4 kHz notch in a noise-exposed worker is a classic and well-recognised pattern, not an artefact. Delaying protection while awaiting a repeat test exposes the worker to continued damage.

overallFeedback.feedback: The 4 kHz dip is the earliest sign of noise-induced hearing loss. In a noise-exposed worker, this is not presbycusis, not conductive loss, and not an artefact. The correct response is hearing protection and periodic audiometry.
Correct. The 4 kHz notch is the hallmark of noise-induced hearing loss and a medicolegal marker for occupational compensation. Protection and follow-up must begin immediately.
